tips.title: Learn the definition word for word
tips.body: Cyber security is **the processes, practices and technologies designed to protect networks, computers, programs and data from attack, damage or unauthorised access**. It is the specification's own wording, so it is worth memorising.

tips.title: Seven threats, and one of them is people
tips.body: The list is: **Social engineering, Malicious code, Pharming, Weak and default passwords, Misconfigured access rights, Removable media, Unpatched and/or outdated software**. Notice that the first is about **people**, not technology — which is why it has a section of its own.

tips.title: Pharming redirects, phishing asks
tips.body: **Pharming** redirects a website's traffic to a **fake website** — the victim types the right address and still arrives at the wrong place. **Phishing** sends a message **asking** for details. One hijacks the route; the other asks nicely.

tips.title: A trojan is defined by disguise
tips.body: A **virus** spreads by attaching to files. A **trojan** does not spread itself — it **pretends to be something useful** so the user installs it willingly. The difference is how it gets in, not what it does afterwards.

tips.title: Two pen tests, two attackers
tips.body: Testing **with** knowledge or credentials simulates a **malicious insider**. Testing **without** any simulates an **external attack**. Say which attacker each one imitates, not just what the tester knows.

why.matters:
Every system worth attacking is attacked, constantly and mostly automatically, and the specification is precise about what defending it means: the **processes, practices and technologies** designed to protect networks, computers, programs and data from attack, damage or unauthorised access.

Three words, not one. Technology is only a third of it, and the list of threats makes that obvious — several of them involve nothing being broken into at all. A default password, an access right nobody revoked, an update nobody installed.

examples.title: Why a USB stick walks straight past the firewall
examples.body:
A firewall inspects what crosses the network. Removable media never crosses it: somebody carries the data through the front door in a pocket and plugs it in on the inside, where everything trusts everything.

That is why it is on the list of threats in its own right. It is also why the defences against it are rules about people rather than more equipment, and why an organisation that has spent heavily on its network can still be undone by a stick found in a car park.

visual.alt: A table of three ways malware arrives: a download and an email attachment both cross the network where a firewall can inspect them, while a USB stick does not cross it at all

examples.title: Why a trojan does not have to break anything
examples.body:
Malware is an umbrella term. A virus and a trojan, two of the forms the specification names, differ in **how they arrive**. A virus attaches to a file and travels when that file is opened or shared. A trojan is disguised as something useful, so the user installs it willingly — the defences are not broken, they are walked through.

Spyware is defined instead by what it does, and it is the quiet one: usually hidden inside software the user installed, it records what is typed and sends it back, which is why encryption on the connection does not help. The password is captured before it is ever encrypted.

rows: hidden inside software the user installs

visual.alt: A table of the three forms of malware: a virus attaches to a file and spreads when it is opened, a trojan is disguised so the user installs it, and spyware secretly records what the user does, arriving hidden inside other software

examples.title: Why a published patch makes an unpatched machine easier to attack
examples.body:
A patch is an announcement. It says what the flaw was and roughly where, so the day it is published the flaw stops being a secret — and every machine that has not installed it becomes a **known** target rather than a guess.

So "unpatched and outdated software" is a threat that grows over time, which is the opposite of how people treat it. It is also why automatic updates are one of the five measures the specification names: the gap between a patch existing and a patch being installed is the whole window.

visual.alt: A table of what a published patch changes: before it the flaw is unknown and finding it takes skill, after it the flaw is public and any machine without the patch is a known target

steps.title: What cyber security is
steps.body:
**The specification gives a definition worth learning exactly:**

> **Cyber security consists of the processes, practices and technologies designed to protect networks, computers, programs and data from attack, damage or unauthorised access.**

Three things in that are worth noticing.

**It is not only technology.** **Processes** and **practices** — how an organisation works, what its staff are trained to do — sit alongside the technology. A company with excellent firewalls and untrained staff is not secure.

**It protects four things**: networks, computers, programs and data.

**Against three things**: attack, damage and unauthorised access. Note that **damage** need not be deliberate — an accidental deletion is a security failure too.

**The purposes of cyber security** are usually summarised as keeping data **confidential** (only those allowed can see it), **accurate** (nobody can alter it without authority), and **available** (those entitled to it can get at it when needed).

That last one is often forgotten. A system nobody can break into but nobody can use has also failed.

visuals.alt: A four-box card giving the definition of cyber security, what it protects, against what, and its purposes

check.prompt: According to the specification, what does cyber security consist of?
options: The laws governing computer misuse
Firewalls and antivirus software only
Processes, practices and technologies
Encryption applied to stored data
check.solution: **Processes, practices and technologies** designed to protect networks, computers, programs and data. Technology alone is not the whole of it — how people work matters just as much.

steps.title: The seven threats
steps.body:
**The specification lists seven threats you must be able to explain.**

**Social engineering techniques** — manipulating **people** into giving up confidential information. This is large enough to have its own section, covering blagging, phishing and shouldering.

**Malicious code (malware)** — hostile or intrusive software, covered in the next step.

**Pharming** — the specification's definition: **a cyber attack intended to redirect a website's traffic to a fake website**. The victim types the correct address and still lands somewhere false, where their details are captured.

**Weak and default passwords** — `password123`, or a router left on the factory password printed in its manual. Default passwords are published online, so a device that keeps one is effectively unlocked.

**Misconfigured access rights** — users able to reach data they should not. Often nobody attacks anything: the door was simply left open, and one careless or curious employee finds it.

**Removable media** — a USB stick carries malware **straight past the firewall**, because it never travels over the network at all. It works the other way too: data **copied out** onto a stick leaves with it, and a lost, unencrypted stick hands whatever is on it to whoever finds it.

**Unpatched and/or outdated software** — a known flaw left unfixed. **Outdated** software may no longer receive updates at all, so its flaws can never be fixed. Once a patch is published, the flaw it fixes becomes **public knowledge**, so unpatched machines become **easier** to attack, not harder.

**Notice how many involve no clever technology.** Weak passwords, misconfigured rights and unpatched software are all failures of **process**, which is exactly why the definition mentions processes and practices.

rows: manipulating people into giving up confidential information
hostile or intrusive software installed on a system
redirecting a website's traffic to a fake website
passwords that are easily guessed or never changed from the factory setting
users able to reach data they should not be able to
USB sticks carrying malware in past the defences, or data out
known flaws left unfixed, or software too old to get fixes
props.title: Three of the seven are failures of process rather than attacks

visuals.alt: A table of the seven cyber security threats named in the specification and what each means

check.prompt: Which threat is defined as an attack intended to redirect a website's traffic to a fake website?
check.solution: **Pharming.** The victim enters the correct address but is sent to a fake site, where their details are captured.

steps.title: Malware
steps.body:
**Malware is an umbrella term** used to refer to a variety of forms of **hostile or intrusive software**. The specification names three forms.

**Virus** — attaches itself to a **file**, and spreads when that file is **opened** or shared. It needs the file to travel and the user to run it.

**Trojan** — **disguises itself as something useful** so that the user **installs it willingly**. Named after the wooden horse: the defences are not broken, they are **walked through**. A trojan does **not** spread itself.

**Spyware** — **secretly records what the user does**, such as the keys they press, and sends it back to the attacker. Passwords and card numbers are captured as they are typed, so encryption of the stored data does not help.

**A virus and a trojan differ in how they get in and spread**, not in what they do afterwards: either might steal data or damage files. **Spyware is defined by what it does** — secretly recording what the user does and sending it on. It usually arrives hidden inside other software. A virus **attaches**, a trojan **deceives**, spyware **watches**.

**Protecting against malware:** anti-malware software, a **firewall**, **keeping software up to date**, not opening attachments or installing programs from unknown sources, and **restricting who may install software** at all.

**Backups** belong on that list too. They do not prevent an infection, but they mean a successful one does not have to be a disaster.

damages or deletes files, and spreads
disguised as something useful; the user installs it
opens a way in for the attacker

check.prompt: What distinguishes a trojan from a virus?
options: It damages files rather than stealing information
It is disguised as something useful so the user installs it
It spreads automatically to every computer on a network
It can only infect a computer through removable media
check.solution: A **trojan** pretends to be something the user **wants**, so they install it themselves — the defences are walked through rather than broken. A **virus** attaches to a file and spreads when that file is opened.

steps.title: Penetration testing
steps.body: **The specification defines penetration testing as the process of attempting to gain access to resources without knowledge of usernames, passwords and other normal means of access.** In short: attacking your own system on purpose to find the holes before someone else does.

visuals.problem: Explain what penetration testing is and describe the two types.

steps.text: It is an **authorised** attempt to break into a system, to find weaknesses **before a real attacker does**
steps.note: authorised is the word that separates it from a crime

steps.text: The point is to find what is **actually** exploitable, rather than what is believed to be secure
steps.note: a system is only as secure as its weakest point, which is rarely the one people worry about

steps.text: **First type:** the tester has **knowledge of the system and possibly basic credentials**
That answers: how much damage could someone **already inside** do — an employee, or an attacker who has stolen one password?
steps.note: it tests what lies behind the front door, where access rights are often misconfigured

steps.text: **Second type:** the tester has **no knowledge of any credentials**
That answers: could a stranger with no help get in at all?
steps.note: it tests the front door itself

steps.text: Both are needed, because they test **different** things
steps.note: a strong front door proves nothing about what an insider could reach

rows: knowledge of the system and possibly basic credentials
props.title: The two differ only in what the tester is given at the start

visuals.alt: A table of the two types of penetration testing, what the tester knows and which attacker each simulates

check.prompt: A penetration tester is given no credentials at all. Which attacker does this simulate?
options: An external attack
A malicious insider
An accidental data loss
A hardware failure
check.solution: With **no knowledge of any credentials**, the test simulates an **external attack** — a stranger trying to get in. Testing **with** knowledge or basic credentials simulates a **malicious insider**.

steps.title: Going deeper
steps.body:
**Quote the definition.** *Processes, practices and technologies designed to protect networks, computers, programs and data from attack, damage or unauthorised access.* It is the specification's own wording, and the **processes and practices** half is the part that is easy to forget.

**Keep pharming and phishing apart.** **Pharming redirects** traffic to a **fake website**; **phishing asks** by message. The reason pharming is more dangerous is worth stating: the victim **types the correct address** and has no reason to be suspicious, because nothing they can see is wrong.

**Explain the patch paradox.** When a patch is published, the flaw it fixes becomes **public knowledge**. Attackers read the patch to learn what was wrong, so an unpatched machine is **more** exposed after the fix exists than before. That is why "we'll update it later" is worse than it sounds.

**Say why removable media defeats a firewall.** A firewall inspects traffic **crossing the network boundary**. A USB stick carries data **physically past** it, so the file never comes under inspection at all. Naming the mechanism earns more than naming the threat.

**Define a trojan by disguise, not by damage.** A trojan **pretends to be useful** so the user installs it willingly — the defences are **walked through**, not broken. It does **not** spread itself, which is the clearest difference from a virus.

**Explain spyware's specific danger.** It captures information **as it is typed**, so encrypting stored data protects nothing — the password is taken **before** any encryption happens.

**Match each penetration test to its attacker.** With knowledge or basic credentials → a **malicious insider**. With none → an **external attack**. Add why both are run: a secure front door says nothing about what someone already inside could reach.

**Notice how many threats are not attacks.** Weak and default passwords, misconfigured access rights and unpatched software are failures of **process**. No attacker was clever; a door was left open. Making that observation shows you have understood why the definition mentions processes at all.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- **Cyber security** is the **processes, practices and technologies** designed to protect **networks, computers, programs and data** from **attack, damage or unauthorised access**.
- It aims to keep data **confidential**, **accurate** and **available**.
- The seven threats: **Social engineering techniques**, **Malicious code (malware)**, **Pharming**, **Weak and default passwords**, **Misconfigured access rights**, **Removable media**, **Unpatched and/or outdated software**.
- **Pharming** redirects a website's traffic to a **fake website**.
- **Phishing asks**; **pharming redirects** — the victim types the right address.
- **Default passwords** are published online, so an unchanged one is no protection.
- **Misconfigured access rights** let users reach data they should not.
- **Removable media** carries malware **physically past the firewall**.
- **Unpatched software** is **more** exposed after a patch, because the flaw becomes public.
- **Malware** is an umbrella term for **hostile or intrusive software**.
- A **virus** attaches to a file and spreads when it is opened.
- A **trojan** is **disguised as something useful**, and does not spread itself.
- **Spyware** records what the user does, such as keys pressed.
- **Penetration testing** is attempting to gain access **without** the normal means of access.
- **With** credentials it simulates a **malicious insider**; **without**, an **external attack**.

questions.prompt: Complete the definition: cyber security consists of the processes, ______ and technologies designed to protect networks, computers, programs and data.
questions.solution: Processes, **practices** and technologies. The wording matters — it makes clear that security is not technology alone.

questions.prompt: Which threat redirects a website's traffic to a fake website?
questions.solution: **Pharming.** The victim enters the correct web address and is nonetheless taken to a fake site.

questions.prompt: What is malware?
options: An umbrella term for hostile or intrusive software
A single type of virus that attacks only networks
Any software that has simply become out of date
A weakness found in a password or login system
questions.solution: Malware is an **umbrella term** covering a variety of forms of **hostile or intrusive software** — viruses, trojans and spyware among them.

markScheme.description: an umbrella term for hostile software

questions.prompt: Which of these is a form of malware named in the specification?
options: Spyware
Pharming
Shouldering
Blagging
questions.solution: **Spyware**, along with viruses and trojans. Pharming is a separate threat, and shouldering and blagging are forms of **social engineering**.

questions.prompt: What does spyware do?
options: Disguises itself as a useful program to be installed
Secretly records what the user does, such as keys pressed
Attaches itself to a file and spreads when it is opened
Redirects the user to a fake version of a website
questions.solution: **Spyware** secretly **records the user's activity**, including keystrokes, and reports back. Disguise describes a **trojan**, attaching to files a **virus**, and redirection is **pharming**.

markScheme.description: secretly records what the user does

questions.prompt: Why is a default password a security risk?
options: Default passwords are published online and are widely known
Default passwords are always shorter than eight characters
A default password cannot be changed by the user
Default passwords stop antivirus software from running
questions.solution: Many devices have shipped with the **same** default on every unit, and those defaults are **published online**. A device left on its factory password is effectively unlocked to anyone who looks it up.

markScheme.description: they are published and widely known

questions.prompt: What is penetration testing?
options: Scanning every file on a system for known malware signatures
Encrypting all data before it is allowed to leave the network
An authorised attempt to get in without the normal access details
Checking that every user's password meets the length rules
questions.solution: The specification defines penetration testing as **attempting to gain access to resources without knowledge of usernames, passwords and other normal means of access**, done with permission to find weaknesses before a real attacker does. Scanning for malware signatures is anti-malware software, encrypting outgoing data is encryption, and checking password length is a password rule.

markScheme.description: an authorised attempt to gain access without the normal means

questions.prompt: What are misconfigured access rights?
options: A website has been replaced with a fake copy
Passwords have been set too short to be secure
Software has not been updated for a long time
Users are able to reach data they should not be able to
questions.solution: Permissions have been set wrongly, so people can reach data they should not. Often nobody attacks anything at all — the door was simply left open.

markScheme.description: users can reach data they should not

questions.prompt: How does a virus spread?
options: It records keystrokes and sends them to an attacker
It is installed by the user believing it to be useful
It attaches to a file and spreads when that file is opened
It redirects web traffic to a copy of a real site
questions.solution: A **virus attaches itself to a file** and spreads when that file is opened or shared. Being installed willingly describes a **trojan**.

markScheme.description: attaches to a file and spreads when opened

questions.prompt: A penetration tester is given a normal employee's login. Which attacker is being simulated?
options: An external attacker
A malicious insider
An automated malware infection
An accidental deletion of data
questions.solution: Testing **with knowledge and possibly basic credentials** simulates a **malicious insider** — someone who already has legitimate access and abuses it.

questions.prompt: Why does unpatched software become more dangerous after the patch is released?
options: The patch reveals the flaw, so attackers learn exactly what to exploit
Patches slow down any computer that has not installed them
Software stops working correctly once a patch exists
The manufacturer withdraws support for the old version
questions.solution: Publishing a patch makes the flaw **public knowledge** — attackers examine the patch to work out precisely what was wrong. An unpatched machine is therefore **more** exposed after the fix exists than before it, which is why delaying updates is worse than it sounds.

markScheme.description: the patch makes the flaw public

questions.prompt: Why is a USB stick a threat even to a network protected by a firewall?
options: Firewalls only inspect traffic between two internal computers
Firewalls are switched off whenever a USB device is used
USB sticks can disable a firewall once they are inserted
The file never crosses the network, so the firewall never inspects it
questions.solution: A firewall inspects traffic **crossing the network boundary**. A USB stick carries the file **physically past** it, so it is never examined. The defence was not defeated — it was simply walked around.

markScheme.description: the file never crosses the network

questions.prompt: Why is pharming considered more dangerous than phishing?
options: Phishing requires the attacker to know the victim personally
Pharming can only be carried out against large companies
The victim types the correct address, so nothing looks wrong
Pharming installs malware directly onto the victim's computer
questions.solution: Phishing relies on the victim **following a link** in a message, which a careful person may spot. Pharming **redirects the traffic itself**, so the victim enters the **correct** address and still arrives at the fake site — there is nothing visible to be suspicious of.

markScheme.description: the victim types the right address

questions.prompt: Why does encrypting stored passwords not protect against spyware?
options: Spyware can decrypt any password that has been stored
Spyware captures the password as it is typed, before encryption
Encryption is switched off while a user is logging in
Spyware replaces the encryption software on the computer
questions.solution: Spyware records the **keys as they are pressed**, which happens **before** anything is stored or encrypted. The protection is applied at the wrong point in the chain to help — which is why anti-malware, not encryption, is the defence here.

markScheme.description: it captures the password before encryption

questions.prompt: Why would an organisation carry out both an insider (with credentials) and an external (no credentials) penetration test, rather than only one?
options: The second test confirms the results of the first one
Running two separate tests is required by law for every organisation
They test different things: the way in, and the reach inside
One tests the hardware and the other tests the software
questions.skill: why both pen tests are run
questions.solution: The **external** test asks whether a stranger could get in at all. The **insider** test asks how much damage someone who is already in — an employee, or an attacker with one stolen password — could do. A strong front door says nothing about the second question.

questions.prompt: Weak and default passwords, misconfigured access rights and unpatched software are three of the cyber security threats the specification lists, and none of them needs a clever attacker. Which observation does this support?
options: Technology has made the other four threats obsolete
Most organisations do not need to buy any security technology at all
Attackers rarely bother to target small organisations
Security needs processes and practices, not just technology
questions.solution: Weak and default passwords, misconfigured access rights and unpatched software are all failures of **process** — a door left open rather than one forced. This is exactly why the specification's definition names **processes and practices** alongside technologies.

markScheme.description: security depends on processes, not technology alone

questions.prompt: Explain what malware is, describe the three forms named in the specification, and explain how a system can be protected against it.
questions.solution:
**Malware** is an **umbrella term** used to refer to a variety of forms of **hostile or intrusive software**. It is not one thing but a category, and the specification names three forms.

A **virus attaches itself to a file** and spreads when that file is **opened** or shared. It needs a host file to travel in and a user to run it, and it may then damage or delete data as well as spreading further.

A **trojan disguises itself as something useful** — a game, a utility, an attachment that appears legitimate — so that the user **installs it willingly**. It is named after the wooden horse for good reason: the defences are not broken, they are **walked through**. Unlike a virus, a trojan does **not** spread itself; it relies entirely on persuading each user in turn.

**Spyware secretly records what the user does**, typically the **keys they press**, and sends that information back to the attacker. Passwords, card numbers and messages are all captured as they are typed.

**A virus and a trojan are told apart by how they get in and spread**, not by the damage they do: either might steal data or damage files once installed. **Spyware** is defined by what it does — secretly recording and reporting back — and usually arrives hidden inside other software, sometimes by way of a trojan. A virus **attaches**, a trojan **deceives**, and spyware **watches**.

**Protection** works at several points. **Anti-malware software** scans files and running programs against known threats and behaviour, catching infections that are already recognised. A **firewall** monitors incoming and outgoing traffic and blocks what its rules do not permit. **Keeping software up to date** closes known flaws — and matters more than it sounds, because once a patch is published the flaw it fixes becomes **public knowledge**, leaving unpatched machines more exposed than before.

Other measures target the way malware actually arrives. **Not opening attachments or installing software from unknown sources** addresses the trojan directly, since a trojan cannot install itself. **Restricting who may install software** limits the damage a single careless user can do. Controlling the use of **removable media** matters because a USB stick carries files **physically past the firewall**, which never inspects them.

**Backups** belong on the list as well. They prevent nothing, but they mean a successful attack — particularly one that destroys or encrypts data — need not be a disaster.

Note that against **spyware** specifically, encrypting stored passwords does not help: the keystrokes are captured **as they are typed**, before anything is stored, so the protection is applied at the wrong point in the chain.

criteria.text: Defines malware and describes a virus and a trojan.
Describes spyware and distinguishes the three clearly.
Explains protective measures and why they work.

questions.prompt: A company suffers a data breach. Explain the threats that could have caused it and describe how penetration testing could have helped prevent it.
questions.solution:
Several of the threats in the specification could account for a breach, and they are worth separating into **attacks** and **failures of process**.

Among the **attacks**: **social engineering** could have persuaded an employee to hand over their login, since manipulating a person needs no technical weakness at all. **Malware** — a **trojan** disguised as a useful program, or **spyware** capturing passwords as they were typed — could have given the attacker credentials. **Pharming** could have redirected staff to a fake version of a login page, where the victim would type the **correct** address and still surrender their details.

Among the **failures of process**: **weak or default passwords** may simply have been guessed, and default passwords are **published online**, so an unchanged one is effectively no password. **Misconfigured access rights** might have meant an ordinary employee could already reach data they had no business seeing, in which case no attack was needed. **Unpatched software** could have left a known flaw open — and once a patch exists the flaw becomes **public knowledge**, so delay makes a system **more** exposed, not less. **Removable media** could have carried malware **physically past the firewall**, which never inspects a file that does not cross the network.

**Penetration testing** is the **authorised** process of attempting to gain access to resources **without knowledge of usernames, passwords and other normal means of access** — attacking your own system deliberately to find what is genuinely exploitable, rather than what is assumed to be safe.

The specification describes **two types**. In the first, the tester has **knowledge of the system and possibly basic credentials**, simulating **a malicious insider**. In the second, the tester has **no knowledge of any credentials**, simulating an **external attack**.

**How testing would have helped** depends on which weakness was exploited, which is exactly why both types are run. An **external** test would have tried to get in from outside with nothing to start from, and would likely have found **default passwords** on exposed devices and **unpatched software** with known public flaws. An **insider** test, starting from an ordinary employee account, would have revealed **misconfigured access rights** — showing how far a single compromised login could actually reach.

The insider test is easy to leave out, and it is the one that matters most here. A company can have an impeccable front door and still lose everything if one stolen password opens the whole building. Testing only from outside would have confirmed the perimeter was strong while leaving that entirely unexamined.

It is worth being honest about the limits, though. Penetration testing finds **technical** weaknesses well, but the threat it addresses least directly is **social engineering**, because that attacks **people** rather than systems. A company relying on pen testing alone would still need **staff training**, which is precisely why the definition of cyber security names **processes and practices** alongside technologies.

markScheme.description: penetration testing and its two types

criteria.text: Identifies several relevant threats and explains how each could cause a breach.
Explains penetration testing and describes both types.
Explains how testing would have found the weaknesses, with judgement.

questions.modelAnswer:
Several of the threats in the specification could account for a breach, and they are worth separating into **attacks** and **failures of process**.

Among the **attacks**: **social engineering** could have persuaded an employee to hand over their login, since manipulating a person needs no technical weakness at all. **Malware** — a **trojan** disguised as a useful program, or **spyware** capturing passwords as they were typed — could have given the attacker credentials. **Pharming** could have redirected staff to a fake version of a login page, where the victim would type the **correct** address and still surrender their details.

Among the **failures of process**: **weak or default passwords** may simply have been guessed, and default passwords are **published online**, so an unchanged one is effectively no password. **Misconfigured access rights** might have meant an ordinary employee could already reach data they had no business seeing, in which case no attack was needed. **Unpatched software** could have left a known flaw open — and once a patch exists the flaw becomes **public knowledge**, so delay makes a system **more** exposed, not less. **Removable media** could have carried malware **physically past the firewall**, which never inspects a file that does not cross the network.

**Penetration testing** is the **authorised** process of attempting to gain access to resources **without knowledge of usernames, passwords and other normal means of access** — attacking your own system deliberately to find what is genuinely exploitable, rather than what is assumed to be safe.

The specification describes **two types**. In the first, the tester has **knowledge of the system and possibly basic credentials**, simulating **a malicious insider**. In the second, the tester has **no knowledge of any credentials**, simulating an **external attack**.

**How testing would have helped** depends on which weakness was exploited, which is exactly why both types are run. An **external** test would have tried to get in from outside with nothing to start from, and would likely have found **default passwords** on exposed devices and **unpatched software** with known public flaws. An **insider** test, starting from an ordinary employee account, would have revealed **misconfigured access rights** — showing how far a single compromised login could actually reach.

The insider test is easy to leave out, and it is the one that matters most here. A company can have an impeccable front door and still lose everything if one stolen password opens the whole building. Testing only from outside would have confirmed the perimeter was strong while leaving that entirely unexamined.

It is worth being honest about the limits, though. Penetration testing finds **technical** weaknesses well, but the threat it addresses least directly is **social engineering**, because that attacks **people** rather than systems. A company relying on pen testing alone would still need **staff training**, which is precisely why the definition of cyber security names **processes and practices** alongside technologies.

questions.prompt: Which of these is one of the main purposes of cyber security?
options: Making every program on a computer run more quickly
Cutting the amount of electricity a network uses
Giving every user the same access rights to all data
Keeping data private, correct and available when needed
questions.solution: Cyber security aims to keep data **confidential** (only those allowed can see it), **accurate** (nobody alters it without authority) and **available** to those entitled to it. Speed and energy use are not its purpose, and giving everyone the same access would undo the confidentiality it protects.

questions.prompt: A school wants to stop trojans being installed on its computers. Which measure targets the way a trojan gets in?
options: Backing up every computer's files each week
Only letting administrators install new software
Encrypting the files stored on the school server
Adding a CAPTCHA to the school's login page
questions.solution: A **trojan** gets in by persuading a user to **install it willingly**, so **restricting who may install software** closes that route. Backups help recovery but prevent nothing, encryption stops stored files being read, and a CAPTCHA blocks automated programs at a login page.

questions.prompt: An employee copies customer records onto a USB stick to work at home, and loses the stick on the train. Which measure would most reduce the harm?
options: A firewall on the office's connection to the internet
Anti-malware software running on every office computer
Encrypting the stick, so the records cannot be read
Making every member of staff change passwords monthly
questions.solution: Removable media is a threat in **both** directions: malware can come **in** on it, and data can go **out** on it. Here the data has left the building, so defences on the office network — a **firewall**, **anti-malware**, password changes — never see it. **Encrypting** the stick means whoever finds it holds data they **cannot read**. (A rule against copying such records onto sticks at all would be better still.)

examTechnique.body:
Quote the definition, including **processes and practices**, not technologies alone. Keep **pharming** (redirects to a fake site) apart from **phishing** (asks by message).

Define a **trojan** by its **disguise**, not its damage. Match each penetration test to the attacker it simulates: **with** credentials is an **insider**, **without** is **external**.
examinerErrors: Defining cyber security as technology alone.
Describing a trojan by what it damages rather than its disguise.
Saying a trojan spreads itself like a virus.
Naming removable media without saying it bypasses the firewall.
Missing that a published patch makes the flaw public.
Describing only one type of penetration testing.
Forgetting that penetration testing must be authorised.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer quotes the definition with **processes, practices and technologies**, and notices that several listed threats — weak passwords, misconfigured rights, unpatched software — are **failures of process** rather than clever attacks. It separates **pharming** from **phishing** by saying the victim **types the correct address**, defines a **trojan** by **disguise** and notes it does **not** spread itself, and explains why encryption cannot stop **spyware** (the keystroke is captured **before** anything is stored). On penetration testing it names **both** types with the attacker each simulates, says why both are needed, and concedes what testing cannot find: **social engineering**, which attacks people rather than systems.
